title: SQLite WAL: an application team's enablement decision
topic: SQLite WAL mode for an application team deciding whether to enable it: reader/writer interaction, checkpoints, durability, limitations and practical decision guidance; focused, sqlite.org documentation first
scope: Focused public-documentation research for an application team: explain WAL mechanics and reader/writer interaction, checkpoint policy and operations, durability settings, deployment limitations, safe enablement and version caveats. Prefer sqlite.org primary documentation; no workload benchmark or application-specific validation. Assumed local-host file-backed database. Eight questions across four sections keep this narrow request focused.
prose_review: not independently reviewed at light depth

sections.name: How WAL changes reader and writer interaction

questions.question: How does a WAL commit work, what snapshot do readers see, and how many writers can run?

headline.sentence: WAL gives readers stable snapshots alongside a writer; writes still serialize.

answer.sentence: SQLite appends changed pages and a commit record to the WAL, allowing a commit without first copying those changes into the main database file.
Each read transaction keeps its own commit end mark: it reads the latest eligible page from the WAL, or falls back to the main database, so later commits do not change its snapshot.
Readers and a writer can run together, but only one writer can hold the database's write transaction at a time.

questions.question: Which contention and stale-snapshot cases remain, and what transaction practices follow?

headline.sentence: Handle lock contention and restart stale read-to-write transactions.

answer.sentence: A transaction that reads an old snapshot and later tries to write can receive SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT; it must release that snapshot and begin a new transaction.

BEGIN IMMEDIATE acquires the write transaction up front for read-then-write work, preventing competing writers from invalidating that transaction's snapshot; it can itself return SQLITE_BUSY if another writer is active.
Queries can also return SQLITE_BUSY during exclusive locking, last-connection cleanup, or crash recovery.
Implicit transactions finish when their last active statement finishes; resetting or finalizing statements guarantees completion.

questions.question: What does a checkpoint do, when do automatic checkpoints run, and how do PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE differ?

headline.sentence: Checkpoints copy committed WAL content into the database; the default policy favors nonblocking progress.

answer.sentence: By default, commits reaching 1000 WAL pages trigger an automatic checkpoint; the threshold is adjustable or can be disabled.
PASSIVE, used automatically, copies what it can without waiting for readers or writers and may leave work unfinished.
FULL waits for the writer and sufficiently current reader snapshots, then checkpoints and syncs on success; it blocks new writers while allowing readers.
RESTART additionally waits until readers no longer need WAL content so the next writer can reuse the beginning; TRUNCATE additionally shrinks the WAL to zero bytes on success.
If the busy handler stops waiting, these aggressive modes can return SQLITE_BUSY with only partial progress.

questions.question: Why can WAL grow or commits stall, and what should a team monitor or tune?

headline.sentence: Watch checkpoint progress and long transactions, not just the WAL's physical file size.

answer.sentence: Overlapping read transactions can prevent WAL reset, disabled checkpoints permit continued growth, and a large write transaction cannot reset the WAL before it finishes.
A completed checkpoint normally enables recycling the existing WAL space rather than shrinking the file, so a large file alone does not prove checkpoint failure.
PRAGMA wal_checkpoint reports a busy indicator, WAL page count, and checkpointed page count to assess progress.
Automatic checkpoints run in the committing thread by default and can make occasional commits much slower; periodic checkpoints can instead run in another thread or process.

questions.question: How do synchronous FULL, NORMAL and OFF affect WAL durability and consistency after application crash versus power or operating-system failure?

headline.sentence: Choose FULL when acknowledged commits must survive power loss; NORMAL trades that durability for fewer syncs.

answer.sentence: In WAL mode, synchronous=FULL adds a WAL sync after each transaction commit and provides atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability.
With synchronous=NORMAL, syncs occur around checkpoints and WAL reuse rather than most transactions; the database stays consistent, but power loss or an OS crash can roll back committed transactions.
An application crash alone does not lose committed transactions under NORMAL; synchronous=OFF also survives an application crash, but power loss or OS failure can corrupt the database.
Durability assumes the operating system and storage actually honor SQLite's synchronization requests.

questions.question: What must the team know about recovery, sidecar files, backups and safe database copying?

headline.sentence: Treat the WAL as database state and use SQLite's live backup facilities.

answer.sentence: A commit does not require a checkpoint, so committed data can still reside in the WAL rather than the main database file.

Separating the database from its WAL while copying or moving it can lose committed transactions or corrupt the database; copying the main file alone is unsafe when committed changes remain in the WAL.
SQLite documents the Online Backup API and VACUUM INTO for backing up a live database.
After the last connection crashes, the first new connection performs recovery under an exclusive lock, and concurrent queries can receive SQLITE_BUSY.

questions.question: When is WAL a good fit, how is it enabled and verified, which connection settings need care, and which current version caveat matters?

headline.sentence: WAL is a candidate for local applications needing reader/writer overlap, with explicit durability and checkpoint policies.

answer.sentence: Decision implication (inference): WAL improves reader/writer overlap, but does not add parallel writers, and mostly-read applications that seldom write can be slightly slower.
Enable with PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL and check that the returned mode is wal; the mode persists across reopenings and applies to all connections to that database file.
Automatic checkpoint configuration belongs to each connection; a busy timeout likewise installs a connection's busy handler and replaces any previous handler.

Version check: SQLite fixed the rare WAL-reset corruption race in 3.51.3 and later, with backports in 3.44.6 and 3.50.7; it affects concurrent connections attempting writes or checkpoints simultaneously.

questions.question: What limitations affect network filesystems, multiple databases, page size, read-only use, transaction size and write-heavy workloads?

headline.sentence: WAL requires local-host access and has operational limits beyond write serialization.

answer.sentence: All database users must run on the same host; WAL does not work over network filesystems.
Updates spanning ATTACHed databases are atomic per database but not across the set, and page_size changes require leaving WAL for a rollback journal mode.
Read-only WAL support began in SQLite 3.22.0 and requires readable existing sidecars, permission to create them, or an immutable connection.
The old large-transaction efficiency limitation was removed in 3.11.0; large write transactions can still create large WAL files, and write-heavy workloads remain constrained by the single writer.

facts.statement: Each SQLite WAL reader retains its last-valid-commit end mark throughout the transaction, yielding a stable snapshot.

citations.quote:
each reader can potentially have its own end mark. But for any

particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the

transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees

the database content as it existed at a single point in time.

facts.statement: A SQLite WAL reader uses the latest page copy before its end mark, falling back to the original database when no eligible WAL copy exists.

citations.quote:
When a reader needs a page of content, it first checks the WAL to

see if that page appears there, and if so it pulls in the last copy

of the page that occurs in the WAL prior to the reader's end mark.

If no copy of the page exists in the WAL prior to the reader's end mark,

then the page is read from the original database file.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL allows readers and a writer to operate concurrently but permits only one writer at a time.

citations.quote:
Writers merely append new content to the end of the WAL file.

Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of

readers, writers and readers can run at the same time. However,

since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at

a time.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL queries can still return SQLITE_BUSY during exclusive locking, last-connection cleanup, or crash recovery.

citations.quote:
If another database connection has the database mode open

in exclusive locking mode then all queries against the

database will return SQLITE_BUSY.
citations.locator: 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode

citations.quote:
When the last connection to a particular database is closing,

that connection will acquire an exclusive lock for a short time while

it cleans up the WAL and shared-memory files. If a separate attempt

is made to open and query the database while the first connection is

still in the middle of its cleanup process, the second connection

might get an SQLITE_BUSY error.
citations.locator: 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode

citations.quote:
If the last connection to a database crashed, then the first new

connection to open the database will start a recovery process. An

exclusive lock is held during recovery. So if a third database connection

tries to jump in and query while the second connection is running recovery,

the third connection will get an SQLITE_BUSY error.
citations.locator: 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode

facts.statement: A SQLite WAL read-to-write upgrade from an outdated snapshot fails with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT and requires releasing the snapshot and starting a new transaction.

citations.quote:
The attempt by X to escalate its

transaction from a read transaction to a write transaction fails with an

SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT error because the snapshot of the database being

viewed by X is no longer the latest version of the database. If X were

allowed to write, it would fork the history of the database file, which is

something SQLite does not support. In order for X to write to the database,

it must first release its snapshot (using ROLLBACK for example) then

start a new transaction with a subsequent BEGIN.

facts.statement: SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE avoids later stale-snapshot upgrades by starting a write transaction immediately and blocking competing writers.

citations.quote:
If X starts a transaction that will initially only read but X knows it

will eventually want to write and does not want to be troubled with

possible SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT errors that arise because another connection

jumped ahead of it in line, then X can issue BEGIN IMMEDIATE to start

its transaction instead of just an ordinary BEGIN. The BEGIN IMMEDIATE

command goes ahead and starts a write transaction, and thus blocks all

other writers.

facts.statement: SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE can itself fail with SQLITE_BUSY when another connection already has an active write transaction.

citations.quote:
IMMEDIATE causes the database connection to start a new write

immediately, without waiting for a write statement. The

BEGIN IMMEDIATE might fail with SQLITE_BUSY if another write

transaction is already active on another database connection.

facts.statement: SQLite implicit transactions commit when the last active statement finishes; resetting or finalizing prepared statements guarantees statement completion.

citations.quote:
An implicit transaction (a transaction that is started automatically,

not a transaction started by BEGIN) is committed automatically when

the last active statement finishes. A statement finishes when its

last cursor closes, which is guaranteed to happen when the

prepared statement is reset or

finalized.

facts.statement: A SQLite checkpoint transfers committed WAL transactions back into the database file.

citations.quote:
Moving
the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a
"checkpoint".

facts.statement: SQLite automatically checkpoints at commits reaching 1000 WAL pages by default; applications can adjust or disable this threshold.

citations.quote:
By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT
occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the
last database connection on a database file closes.

The automatic checkpoint
threshold can be changed or automatic checkpointing can be completely
disabled using the wal_autocheckpoint pragma or by calling the
sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() C interface.

facts.statement: SQLite automatic checkpoints use PASSIVE mode, which makes available progress without waiting for readers or writers and may finish incompletely.

citations.quote: All automatic checkpoints are PASSIVE.

Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database
readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames
in the log were checkpointed.

On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished
if there are concurrent readers or writers.

facts.statement: SQLite FULL checkpoints wait for the writer and sufficiently current reader snapshots, then checkpoint and sync; they block new writers while allowing readers.

citations.quote:
This mode blocks (it invokes the
busy-handler callback) until there is no
database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database
snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the
database file. This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending,
but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

facts.statement: SQLite RESTART additionally waits for readers to finish using the WAL, and TRUNCATE also shrinks it to zero bytes; busy-handler refusal can instead leave either incomplete with SQLITE_BUSY.

citations.quote:
This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL with the addition
that after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the
busy-handler callback)
until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures
that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the
addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior
to a successful return.

If the busy-handler returns 0 before
the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the
checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as
SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible
without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL growth can persist when overlapping readers prevent reset, automatic checkpoints are disabled, or a large write transaction prevents resetting the WAL until it finishes.

citations.quote:
However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers
and there is always at least one active reader, then
no checkpoints will be able to complete
and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

If an application disables the
automatic checkpoint, then there is nothing to prevent the WAL file
from growing excessively.

the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write
transaction. So a large change to a large database
might result in a large WAL file.

facts.statement: SQLite normally recycles the WAL by overwriting from its beginning rather than truncating it, so checkpoint completion does not ordinarily reduce its physical file size.

citations.quote:
The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file
(unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely
causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

facts.statement: SQLite runs automatic checkpoints in the committing thread by default, making some commits much slower; applications can move periodic checkpoints to another thread or process.

citations.quote:
By default, the checkpoint will be
run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes
the WAL over its size limit. This has the effect of causing most
COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger
a checkpoint) to be much slower. If that effect is undesirable, then
the application can disable automatic checkpointing and run the
periodic checkpoints in a separate thread, or separate process.

facts.statement: In WAL mode, synchronous=FULL syncs the WAL after each transaction commit and provides atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.

citations.quote:
FULL is atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable (ACID) in WAL mode and
is atomic, consistent, and isolated with a rollback journal.

With synchronous=FULL in WAL mode, an additional
sync operation of the WAL file happens after each transaction commit.
The extra WAL sync following each transaction helps ensure that
transactions are durable across a power loss.

facts.statement: WAL with synchronous=NORMAL remains consistent, but committed transactions may roll back after power loss or a system crash; transactions survive application crashes.

citations.quote:
WAL mode is always consistent
with synchronous=NORMAL, but WAL mode does lose durability. A transaction
committed in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL might roll back following
a power loss or system crash. Transactions are durable across application
crashes regardless of the synchronous setting or journal mode.

facts.statement: With synchronous=OFF, SQLite skips syncing; an application crash leaves data safe, but operating-system failure or power loss can corrupt the database.

citations.quote:
With synchronous OFF (0), SQLite continues without syncing
as soon as it has handed data off to the operating system.
If the application running SQLite crashes, the data will be safe, but
the database might become corrupted if the operating system
crashes or the computer loses power before that data has been written
to non-volatile storage.

facts.statement: With synchronous=NORMAL in WAL mode, synchronization occurs around checkpoints and WAL reuse rather than during most transactions.

citations.quote:
In WAL mode when synchronous is NORMAL (1), the WAL file is
synchronized before each checkpoint and the database file is
synchronized after each completed checkpoint and the WAL file
header is synchronized when a WAL file begins to be reused after
a checkpoint, but no sync operations occur during most transactions.

facts.statement: SQLite durability relies on the operating system and storage honoring synchronization requests; SQLite assumes flush or fsync waits for pending file writes to finish.

citations.quote:
SQLite assumes that the flush or fsync will not return until
all pending write operations for the file that is being flushed have
completed.

facts.statement: The WAL file is persistent database state; separating it from the database during copying or moving can lose committed transactions or corrupt the database.

citations.quote:
The WAL file is part of the persistent state of the
database and should be kept with the database if the database is copied
or moved. If a database file is separated from its WAL file, then
transactions that were previously committed to the database might be lost,
or the database file might become corrupted.

facts.statement: After the last connection crashes, the first new connection performs recovery while holding an exclusive lock, and concurrent queries can receive SQLITE_BUSY.

citations.quote:
If the last connection to a database crashed, then the first new
connection to open the database will start a recovery process. An
exclusive lock is held during recovery. So if a third database connection
tries to jump in and query while the second connection is running recovery,
the third connection will get an SQLITE_BUSY error.
citations.locator: 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode

facts.statement: SQLite documents the Online Backup API and VACUUM INTO as methods for backing up a live database.

citations.quote:
The Online Backup API is the original method for making backups of a
live SQLite databases. Other more recent techniques for accomplishing
the same thing include:
The VACUUM INTO command will make a vacuumed copy of a live
SQLite database into a separate file.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL permits concurrent readers and a writer, but can be slightly slower for applications that mostly read and seldom write.

citations.quote:
WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and 
 a writer does not block readers. Reading and writing can proceed 
 concurrently.

WAL might be very slightly slower (perhaps 1% or 2% slower)
 than the traditional rollback-journal approach
 in applications that do mostly reads and seldom write.

facts.statement: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL enables WAL only if the returned journal mode is wal; conversion can fail when the VFS lacks shared-memory support.

citations.quote:
PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;

The journal_mode pragma returns a string which is the new journal mode.
On success, the pragma will return the string "wal". If 
the conversion to WAL could not be completed (for example, if the VFS
does not support the necessary shared-memory primitives) then the
journaling mode will be unchanged and the string returned from the
primitive will be the prior journaling mode (for example "delete").

facts.statement: WAL mode persists across database reopenings and applies to all connections accessing the same database file.

citations.quote:
Unlike the other journaling modes, 
PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL is
persistent. If a process sets WAL mode, then closes and reopens the
database, the database will come back in WAL mode.

The WAL journal mode will be set on all
connections to the same database file if it is set on any one connection.

facts.statement: Every new SQLite connection starts with automatic checkpointing enabled at the default threshold, so checkpoint configuration is connection-specific.

citations.quote:
Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint
enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT
pages.

facts.statement: A SQLite busy timeout installs a connection's busy handler to wait before returning SQLITE_BUSY and replaces any existing handler.

citations.quote:
This routine sets a busy handler that sleeps
for a specified amount of time when a table is locked. The handler
will sleep multiple times until at least "ms" milliseconds of sleeping
have accumulated. After at least "ms" milliseconds of sleeping,
the handler returns 0 which causes sqlite3_step() to return
SQLITE_BUSY.

There can only be a single busy handler for a particular
database connection at any given moment. If another busy handler
was defined (using sqlite3_busy_handler()) prior to calling
this routine, that other busy handler is cleared.

facts.statement: SQLite fixed the rare WAL-reset corruption race in 3.51.3 and later, with backports in 3.44.6 and 3.50.7.

citations.quote:
The bug is likely present in all version of SQLite from
3.7.0 (2010-07-21) through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09). It is
fixed in version 3.51.3 (2026-03-13) and later. Backports of the fix
are available for some earlier releases:
3.44.6 and
3.50.7.

Changes in this specific patch release, version 3.51.3 (2026-03-13):

 Fix the WAL-reset database corruption bug.
citations.locator: Changes in this specific patch release

facts.statement: The WAL-reset bug affects concurrent connections in separate threads or processes that attempt writing or checkpointing simultaneously.

citations.quote:
The bug only affects databases in WAL mode when there are two or more
database connections open on the same file, in separate threads or processes,
and when those two connections attempt to write or checkpoint at the
same instant.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL requires database users on the same host and does not work over a network filesystem.

citations.quote:
All processes using a database must be on the same host computer;
 WAL does not work over a network filesystem. This is because WAL requires
 all processes to share a small amount of memory and processes on
 separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other.

facts.statement: Transactions updating multiple ATTACHed SQLite databases are atomic per database in WAL mode, but not atomic across the database set.

citations.quote:
Transactions that involve changes against multiple ATTACHed
 databases are atomic for each individual database, but are not
 atomic across all databases as a set.

facts.statement: SQLite cannot change page_size while in WAL mode; changing it requires a rollback journal mode.

citations.quote:
It is not possible to change the page_size after entering WAL
 mode, either on an empty database or by using VACUUM or by restoring
 from a backup using the backup API. You must be in a rollback journal
 mode to change the page size.

facts.statement: Read-only WAL access requires readable existing sidecars, permission to create them, or an immutable connection; this support began in SQLite 3.22.0.

citations.quote:
This constraint was relaxed beginning with
SQLite version 3.22.0 (2018-01-22).

On newer versions of SQLite,
a WAL-mode database on read-only media, or a WAL-mode database that lacks
write permission, can still be read as long as one or more of the following
conditions are met:

The -shm and -wal files already exist and are readable.

There is write permission on the directory containing the database so
 that the -shm and -wal files can be created.

The database connection is opened using the
 immutable query parameter.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL's old large-transaction efficiency limitation was removed in 3.11.0, but large write transactions can still produce large WAL files before checkpointing.

citations.quote:
Beginning with version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), 
 WAL mode works as efficiently with
 large transactions as does rollback mode.

Very large write transactions.
A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, 
which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write
transaction. So a large change to a large database
might result in a large WAL file.

citations.quote:
The wal_checkpoint pragma returns a single row with three
integer columns. The first column is usually 0 but will be
1 if a RESTART or FULL or TRUNCATE checkpoint was blocked from completing,

The second column is the number of modified pages that have been
written to the write-ahead log file.
The third column is the number of pages in the write-ahead log file
that have been successfully moved back into the database file at
